hist2-the-fatherless-the-widow-and-the-s.reason: First paragraph gives Yahweh's measure (the fatherless, widow, stranger, not treasury or army); ends on a research exercise rather than landing what 'strength' means.
hist2-the-fatherless-the-widow-and-the-s.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Does a nation's strength show in its margins? By Yahweh's measure, yes. He does not gauge a people by its treasury or its army but by how it treats the fatherless, the widow and the stranger, the three who have no leverage to make anyone treat them well (Deuteronomy 10:18-19). What a nation does when nothing compels it is what it actually is.
hist2-the-fatherless-the-widow-and-the-s.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Does a nation's strength show in its margins? Yes, because that is where Yahweh looks. He hears the cry of the widow and the orphan whether or not anyone printed it (Exodus 22:22-23), and Jesus said what is done to the least is done to Him (Matthew 25:40). So 1838 is read by asking what the law did for the children, the widows and the people made strangers on the Cherokee road. A nation is as strong as its care for those who cannot compel it, and a history that skips them has skipped the King.

teen.open: Is a country's strength measured by its money or army? Yahweh measures it by how it treats orphans, widows and strangers, the people with no power.
teen.close: So yes, a nation's real strength shows in its margins. Look at how it treated the people who couldn't force anyone to be fair. That's where Yahweh looks, and where Jesus said He stands.

senior.open: Yahweh gave one measure of a nation, and it is not wealth or arms. It is how a people treats the fatherless, the widow and the stranger, who have no means to compel good treatment.
senior.close: So the title's answer stands. A nation's true condition shows in its margins, and reading 1838 by that measure asks one plain question: what did the law of that year do for those three?

hist3-the-landmark-and-the-vineyard.reason: Builds the landmark law and Naboth's story; the answer (a lawful form settles nothing, the charge is filed on substance) only arrives in the last paragraph, then ends on a title-tracing exercise.
hist3-the-landmark-and-the-vineyard.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. If the paperwork was lawful, was the land taken justly? Paperwork alone cannot tell you. Naboth's vineyard was taken through a lawful form at every step, and Yahweh ignored the form and named the substance: "Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?" (1 Kings 21:19). So the question to ask of any transfer is whether a step was doing the work a threat would otherwise do.
hist3-the-landmark-and-the-vineyard.example: ASKING THE NABOTH QUESTION. Take the record this lesson gives. In 1835 a small faction signed the Treaty of New Echota; the Cherokee National Council protested that the signers held no authority; the Senate ratified it by a single vote; and the removal of 1838 went ahead as if the nation had consented. Each step had a form. The Naboth question asks of each one: was this step doing the work a threat would otherwise do? Write your answer beside each date.
hist3-the-landmark-and-the-vineyard.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. The paperwork was lawful, but was the land taken justly? A lawful form settles nothing by itself, because Yahweh filed His charge against Ahab on substance, not on procedure. That test runs both ways: some land was freely bought and fairly paid, and some was taken in the Naboth shape behind a proper wrapper. You find out which by tracing the record and asking the question in writing. Then you hold your ground as a steward who knows its history.

teen.open: If the papers were legal, was the land taken fairly? Not necessarily. Naboth's vineyard was taken with all the right paperwork, and Yahweh still called it murder and theft.
teen.close: So legal paperwork doesn't prove something was fair. Yahweh looks at what really happened. Trace the history of a piece of land you know and ask that question honestly.

senior.open: Lawful paperwork does not by itself make a taking just. Ahab took Naboth's vineyard through a proper legal form, and Yahweh judged the substance, not the procedure.
senior.close: That is the answer the title asks for. Whether land was taken justly is decided by substance, so each step in the record must be weighed by asking whether it did the work a threat would otherwise have done.

hist1-the-standard-before-the-story.reason: Window and standard are named in paragraph one, but why the record must pass to the children is spread over paragraphs two and three; ends on a childhood-memory exercise.
hist1-the-standard-before-the-story.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Whose window are you looking through? Always someone's: in 1607 the deck saw a founding and the shore saw an arrival. So no telling is the measure. The one standard outside every telling is Yahweh's Word, true from the beginning (Psalms 119:160). And the record must pass to the children, because a generation nobody told soon serves what its neighbors serve (Judges 2:10-12). Here is how the Word shows both.
hist1-the-standard-before-the-story.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Whose window are you looking through? Your own, or your teacher's, or someone's on the deck or the shore. That is why the record is measured by Yahweh's Word, which stands outside every telling, and why it is told with dates and with every person named. And it must pass to the children, because the forgetting runs downhill: a generation nobody told is destroyed for lack of knowledge (Hosea 4:6). The telling is what prevents the forgetting. Open every window, measure by the Word, and hand the whole record on.

teen.open: Every story about history is told from someone's point of view. The one standard outside all of them is Yahweh's Word, and the true story has to be passed on to the next generation.
teen.close: So check whose window you're looking through, measure the story by the Word, and pass the whole record on. When nobody tells the next generation, they forget Yahweh within one generation.

senior.open: Every history is told from a window, and both deck and shore may speak truly. The measure that stands outside every telling is the Word, and the record must be handed to the children so they do not forget.
senior.close: So the answer is twofold. Each telling is weighed against Yahweh's one standard, and the full record is passed down, because Judges shows that a generation left untold turns to other gods.

hist4-the-wage-that-could-not-wait.reason: Opening paragraph sets three laws (wage, manstealing, the escaped servant) settled before any ship sailed; ends on an exercise about one documented person without restating the answer.
hist4-the-wage-that-could-not-wait.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Did Yahweh's law already name slavery as theft? Yes. It made stealing a man and selling him a capital crime (Exodus 21:16). It called withholding a worker's wage defrauding and robbing him (Leviticus 19:13). And it forbade handing an escaped servant back to his master (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). The Word had settled all three before any ship sailed for this coast.
hist4-the-wage-that-could-not-wait.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Did Yahweh's law already name slavery as theft? It did, three times over. Chattel slavery stole the person, kept back the wage, and, by the law of 1850, forced the escaped back to his master. Paul names "menstealers" among those contrary to sound doctrine (1 Timothy 1:10), and Jeremiah's woe falls on the one who uses his neighbour's service without wages (Jeremiah 22:13). So put Leviticus 19:13 and Exodus 21:16 beside one documented name. The verdict was written long before the bill of sale.

teen.open: Did Yahweh's law call slavery stealing? Yes. Kidnapping and selling a person was a death-penalty crime, and holding back a worker's pay was called robbery.
teen.close: So the answer is yes: Yahweh's law already called it theft, of the person and of the wage. Find one real name from the record and read those laws beside it.

senior.open: Yahweh's law named it plainly. Stealing and selling a man was a capital crime, withholding a wage was robbery, and the escaped servant was not to be returned.
senior.close: The answer to the title is therefore yes. American chattel slavery broke all three laws for two and a half centuries, and one documented life set beside Exodus 21:16 shows the verdict was already written.

hist5-two-weights-in-one-bag.reason: Opens on the divers-weights law; how a nation hides a second standard (one law written two ways) and why both halves are owed only arrive in paragraphs two and three; ends on a caution and an exercise.
hist5-two-weights-in-one-bag.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How can a nation hide a second standard in plain sight? By writing one law two ways, in its statute book, its courts and its maps, the way a trader keeps a great and a small weight in one bag (Deuteronomy 25:13-14). And why does Yahweh's record demand both halves? Because the second weight and its removal are both the truth, and a history that keeps only one is carrying a weight of its own.
hist5-two-weights-in-one-bag.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How does a nation hide a second standard in plain sight? In dated, public law: three-fifths, Dred Scott, the Black Codes, Plessy, the red-lined maps, each one law written two ways. And why both halves? Because Brown, the Civil Rights Act, the Voting Rights Act and the Fair Housing Act are just as true, and the Word permits pretending neither away. Yahweh calls divers weights an abomination (Proverbs 20:23). The remedy is one weight for everyone, honestly recorded from the day it was written to the day it ended.

teen.open: How can a country hide two standards? By writing one law two ways, one for some people and another for others. Yahweh calls that a false weight, and He wants the whole story told.
teen.close: So the second standard hid in real, dated laws, and real, dated laws removed it. Tell both halves. The fix for two weights is one fair weight for everyone.

senior.open: A nation hides a second standard by writing one law two ways. Yahweh forbade divers weights in the bag and in the court alike, and His record requires both the injury and its repeal to be told.
senior.close: So the title is answered. The second weight was written into dated American law, and dated law removed much of it; the Word demands both halves, and one weight for all.

hist6-the-fields-of-the-fatherless.reason: Opens on the gleaning law and dated losses (Field Order 15, the Bureau, Greenwood); the answer (Yahweh the helper, and the gleaners who went in: churches, schools, societies) arrives only in paragraph three.
hist6-the-fields-of-the-fatherless.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who gleans the fields when the fathers are gone? Yahweh wrote the answer into His law: the forgotten sheaf belongs to the stranger, the fatherless and the widow, and their Redeemer is mighty to plead their cause (Proverbs 23:10-11). In the American record, the gleaners also went in themselves. Freedpeople and widows founded churches, schools and burial societies that became the help on the ground.
hist6-the-fields-of-the-fatherless.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who gleans the fields when the fathers are gone? Yahweh, the helper of the fatherless (Psalms 10:14), through the provision He commanded and the people He moved. The land promised in 1865 was taken back, the Bureau was wound up, and Greenwood was burned; all of that is true. And the gleaners went in anyway: churches in brush arbours, schools that became colleges, lodges that became lenders. Those are where He has always been at work, and the buildings are still standing in your own community.

teen.open: Who takes care of people when their fathers are gone? Yahweh does. He made laws to leave food for them, and in American history, freed families and widows built churches and schools to help each other.
teen.close: So Yahweh is the helper of the fatherless, and He works through people who go into the fields. Find one church or school in your town started that way.

senior.open: When the fathers are gone, Yahweh Himself is the helper of the fatherless. He commanded the harvest to leave provision, and in America the gleaners went in, founding churches, schools and mutual-aid societies.
senior.close: That is the answer to the title. The losses are documented plainly, and so is the help: Yahweh's provision carried by freedpeople, widows and congregations whose work still stands.

hist7-no-respecter-of-persons.reason: Where it came from (Genesis 1:27, Acts 17:26) is answered at once; who held the nation to it (Douglass, the pulpits, the marchers) is in paragraph two, and the ending does not name them again.
hist7-no-respecter-of-persons.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. The nation wrote a standard it did not keep. Where did it come from? From the Word: all are equal because all bear Yahweh's image (Genesis 1:27), and He made of one blood all nations (Acts 17:26). Who held the country to it? Those who knew where it came from: the abolitionist pulpits, Frederick Douglass at Rochester in 1852, and the marchers of the 1950s and 1960s.
hist7-no-respecter-of-persons.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Where did the standard come from, and who held the nation to it? It came from Yahweh, who is no respecter of persons (Acts 10:34). The country borrowed it in 1776 and broke it, and the people it was denied to held it up anyway: the abolitionist pulpits arguing from the Word, Douglass naming the nation a liar to its own words, the marchers who carried the same sentence. Amendment by amendment, the standard judged the nation that wrote it. A true standard cannot be repealed by being broken.

teen.open: The idea that all men are created equal came from the Word: every person bears Yahweh's image. When the country broke that standard, people like Frederick Douglass held it to it.
teen.close: So the standard came from Yahweh, and the people it was denied to held the nation to it, from preachers to marchers. A true standard doesn't go away when it's broken.

senior.open: The equality written in 1776 came from the Word, from the shared image of Yahweh. Those who held the nation to it were the abolitionist pulpits, Frederick Douglass and the marchers who came after.
senior.close: That is the answer the title promised. The standard was Yahweh's, the nation broke it, and those who carried it back to the nation saw it do its work, date by date.

hist8-two-or-three-witnesses.reason: Paragraph one answers plainly (a single narrator is never history by himself; two or three witnesses establish it), and the last paragraph lands it: witnesses gathered, the matter established, He in the midst.
